title: Why the numbers behind John Healey's £35bn Budget black hole don't add up
excerpt: Everyone seems to expect the UK to stick to its commitments on defence spending – I wouldn’t be so sure, says James Moore
content:
The problems just keep mounting up for Chancellor John Healey. The latest comes courtesy of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, the non-partisan think tank whose work is both widely admired and closely followed. It says he needs to find an awful of money.

There’s a number: £35bn in extra tax rises or spending cuts by fiscal year 2030-31 to maintain investment in the NHS and boost defence spending to the targeted 3 per cent of GDP, while keeping other departmental budgets ticking over.

Doing nothing is not an option. Local authorities have been going bust, the roads are full of potholes, the backlog in the courts led to the preposterous (now dropped) idea of scrapping Brits’ right to a jury trial. That’s just for starters. Immigration anyone?

Right now you’re saying, wait, another Budget black hole? After Rachel Reeves soaked everyone? Where’s all the money gone? Except you probably already know the answer. Donald Trump decided to tell his military to bash Iran. Cue a fresh energy crisis, and the flushing down the toilet of every economic forecast of note.

The conflict sharply raised inflation (and expectations of more to come), helped precipitate a bond market crisis, led to fears of multiple interest rate rises, pushed mortgage rates above six per cent.

Inflation increases public sector pay, putting a strain on departmental budgets, and benefit bills, particularly cost of the state pension. The latter is a benefit even if (few) politicians are willing to admit it.

On the flip side, it also increases tax receipts, at least if private sector pay rises commensurately. It hasn’t been doing that lately, in part because the jobs market has got tighter, but we’ll park that one.

The IFS is actually a little more optimistic than some when it comes to the chancellor’s so-called headroom over the fiscal rules covering borrowing put in place by Rachel Reeves (the Burnham administration has intimated that it will stick to them, even if it doesn’t have much choice).

But here’s the problem with headline grabbing figures like that “£35bn”. It is also a forecast, and it is based on various assumptions. One of those is that the government will push defence spending to that three per cent of GDP. An ambition, an aspiration, call it what you will. I wouldn’t bank on it happening in the short term, even though Healey resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over it. The public finances are too challenged. Assumptions can change, and forecasts with them.

I get criticised for being a Jeremiah, but the truth is the IFS ones could get even worse. On the other hand, things could improve. Maybe Trump takes a kicking in the midterms from inflation-battered US voters who are no fans of his war. Perhaps he decides that it’s time to address that. Perhaps one of the Gulf states steps up and constructs a workable peace deal. The UK has surprising many with its resilience – as Mr Healey will remind us, we’re the fastest growing economy in the G7. You see how this works?

Where I am in full agreement with the IFS is that Healey needs to construct a Budget which the bond markets can live with. Andy Burnham may not like it, but Britain relies upon their goodwill.

However, the chancellor may feel he can do that with something less apocalyptic than the IFS suggests. Count on him saying something like “look at France, look at the US, when it comes to borrowing we’re in much better shape than they are” in the hopes that the message gets through.

The key here is the view of the Office for Budgetary Responsibility, which marks his homework, and has been notably easier on previous chancellors than has the IFS.

I think what the latter may criticise as a ‘do-nothing’ – or at least a ‘do-not-much’ – Budget may nevertheless be coming, in the hopes that the economic weather turns sunnier. Chancellors are, as a breed, quite fond of kicking the can down the road. I doubt this one will prove any different.
